catalog_quote: 2.4 Tone. This section describes tone levels in Gumuz and related tone rules using nouns as examples. However, the same rules apply to tonal behavior in verbs. While this section focuses mainly on tone in Northern Gumuz (NoG), the same tonal patterns and rules have been observed in Southern Gumuz (SoG). ... 2.4.1 Tone Levels and Melodies. In Gumuz, there are two contrastive tone levels, H and L. In two syllable nouns, there are four possible tone melodies, HH, LL, HL, and LH, which are most clearly demonstrated in monomorphemic nouns. ... In 3-syllable nouns, however, 8 possible tone melodies are found: HHH, LLL, HLL, HHL, HLH, LLH, LHH, and LHL. ... [abstract, p. iv:] Gumuz tone has two levels, High and Low, with tonal downstep of High. The tonal melody on bound pronominals on verbs indicates transitivity. ... sweep_summary: The search of works with stress or accent in the title for Northern Gumuz (gumu1244, catalog classification tonal on Ahland 2012 sec. 2.4) turned up exactly one keyword item, Wolde-Selassie 2002 'Indigenous resource management of Gumuz under stress in Metekel', which the Glottolog record (opened and saved) marks listed by Glottolog as an ethnographic work; its 'stress' is land-use pressure, not word stress, so relevance = not relevant, priority none. No new linguistic source on Gumuz stress/accent was found: archive.org search returned only the already-held Uzar 1989 Rosetta excerpt; Crossref has no record of Unseth 1989 'Selected aspects of Gumuz phonology' (the original of the record's lone stress remark, still print only, priority medium as before) nor of Wolde-Selassie 2002; academic.oup.com (Ahland 2023 Northern Gumuz sketch, DOI 10.1093/oxfordhb/9780198728542.013.32, paywalled), sil.org and HathiTrust could not be reached by automated download/an automated-access block challenges; The only stress statement read is the held Ahland 2012 p. 16 passage quoting Unseth 1989:625 (stress correlates with and is determined by H tone), which concerns a Southern Gumuz variety and does not supersede the catalog's deciding source. catalog's classification (tonal) stands; nothing to change. download log and updated under

new_statements.quote: In addition to his findings on lexical tone, Unseth also observed a strong correlation between stress and high tone in Gumuz. However, he adds that “though tone and stress are obviously related, stress is (at least partially) determined by tone, not vice versa” (1989:625).
new_statements.citation: Ahland, Colleen Anne. 2012. A Grammar of Northern and Southern Gumuz. PhD dissertation, University of Oregon (Scholars Bank handle 1794/12559), sec. 1.4.2.2 (review of Unseth 1989), printed p. 16 = PDF p. 45.
new_statements.reading: This is the only stress statement in the Gumuz record and it is not new: it is already the catalog's deciding quotation's companion passage. It is second-hand (Ahland reporting Unseth 1989:625), and per Ahland's own dialect assignment Unseth's data are from Sirba Abay, which she classes as Southern Gumuz, so it is a sister-variety observation that stress (if present) is a by-product of H tone; it does not state a word-stress rule for Northern Gumuz. Nothing read in this search of works with stress in the title changes classification tonal. A a full-text search for stress/accent the 477-page dissertation finds no other prosodic use of 'stress'/'accent' (the other hit, line 139, is the 'Between Stress and Tone' conference travel grant).

sources.quote: 'Suprasegmentals. Consonant and vowel length are not phonemic. What is important is tone ... There are two contrasting register tones, high and low. Tone conveys lexical as well as morphological meanings of words. As a result of this, the Gumuz language can be considered to be a tone language. ... the tone bearing units are the vowels and every vowel carries tone.' No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the thesis (a full-text search for stress/accent).
